title: Enhancing Mathematical Reasoning in Turkish Large Language Models with Search-Based Inference and Model Merging
summary: We improve Turkish mathematical reasoning in Large Language Models by combining LoRA fine-tuning, weight-space model merging, and search-based inference. Using Turkish-Llama 8B-DPO with Turkish translations of MetaMath, NuminaMath, and TigerLab, we find data quality beats scale (Mix-30k best among fine-tuned; large MetaMath underperforms). Linear merging delivers the largest gains (GSM8K up to 0.63), while Ties is modest and Breadcrumbs/Slerp degrade. Search with MCTS and Tree of Thoughts improves mean LLM-judge scores for reasoning quality on a 0-100 scale. Limitations include machine translation, limited scale, and search stochasticity.

title: Task-Critical Part Alignment Improves Imitation of Object Interactions
comment: 6 pages, 6 figures. Accepted at ICAR 2025. This is the preprint version; the published version may differ slightly
summary: This paper presents enhancements to the DINOBot framework for imitation learning of object-object interactions. We introduce two key contributions aimed at improving the accuracy and efficiency of alignment in imitation-based robotic tasks. First, we integrate RANdom SAmple Consensus (RANSAC) for outlier rejection during the alignment phase, effectively mitigating the impact of noisy depth data and spurious feature matches. This improves robustness when transferring demonstrations to real-world applications. Second, we refine the semantic correspondence process by focusing on task-relevant interaction regions, ensuring that the learned representation prioritizes critical object features that influence successful manipulation. We evaluated our approach in a range of real-world manipulation tasks, including picking, insertion, shaking, and pouring, using a robotic system. The experimental results demonstrate an overall improvement of 13.8% in task success rates compared to the baseline, along with faster convergence in the alignment process. These results highlight the effectiveness of our enhancements in improving precision and efficiency for object-object interaction imitation in robotics.

title: Trained, Frozen, or Absent: Identifying What a Quantum Layer Contributes to Cross-Sectional Equity Ranking
summary: Hybrid quantumclassical models are increasingly proposed for nancial prediction, but reported gains are rarely separated from the classical components around them. We study a hybrid quantum temporal convolutional network for daily cross-sectional ranking of 2000 Tokyo Stock Exchange equities under a protocol built to make the quantum contribution identiable: six conditions (circuit trained, frozen or absent, a parameter-matched classical surrogate, and the circuit alone, trained or frozen) through one code path; four walk-forward folds with ve seeds; bootstrap intervals, Deated Sharpe Ratios, backtest-overtting probabilities and family-wise error control; ve classical baselines including a gradient-boosted tree; and a locked holdout. On 500 out-of-sample days two one-sided tests place the trained-versus-frozen dierence inside 0.03 annualised Sharpe (p = 0.0055, minimum detectable eect 0.02): the circuit is equivalent to a frozen one, not merely indistinguishable from it. With the circuit as the head's only input the two are equivalent inside 0.25; against the network with no circuit the design resolves only 0.50. No condition is distinguishable from zero (best De-ated Sharpe Ratio 0.17). The holdout reproduces the ablation on a protable window, and 2000 US equities reproduce it where every condition loses money.

title: Evaluating Physically Grounded Procedural Reasoning in VLMs through Real-World Execution: Crochet as a Testbed
summary: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) can generate procedures that look convincing on paper, but do they work in practice? In this paper, we propose crochet as an ideal testbed for physically grounded procedural reasoning in VLMs. Crochet cannot be reliably simulated or automated: the only way to know what a pattern produces is to make it by hand, yet verification is tangible and cheap, requiring nothing but a hook and a ball of yarn. We introduce FoundationChain, a deceptively simple test of procedural reasoning: given an image of a basic crochet object, can VLMs infer how it was made and generate a pattern that produces the same result? We crochet 40 patterns generated by four VLMs by hand. Even at this scale, physical execution not only reveals failures that automated proxies cannot detect, but also enables a more precise diagnosis of their causes and consequences: while models write fluent, convincing patterns, only four are free of errors, and our analysis exposes deficiencies in visual, geometric and procedural reasoning.

title: Evaluating Jev on Arabic: Comparing Decision Models and LLMs Across Arabic Tasks and Dialects
summary: How does Jev compare with other systems on Arabic tasks, and how does its performance change between Modern Standard Arabic (MSA) and dialects? We evaluate 67 systems, including 47 decision models and 20 large language models (LLMs), on 43 tasks across 9 task families using a shared zero-shot protocol. The Arabic-focused frozen suite includes English controls in three parallel resources, which we also remove in a separate descriptive comparison. Jev 1.14.0 achieves a mean task-primary metric of 69.24 on a scale multiplied by 100, compared with 68.77 for Jev 1.13.0 and 71.81 for Gemma-4-31B, the highest-scoring system on this aggregate. Removing the recorded English controls, repeated cross-task items or both leaves the full system order unchanged. Relative performance and gains between Jev versions vary across task families. In content-matched comparisons within Jev 1.14.0, pooled dialect-minus-MSA accuracy gaps range from -7.94 to -0.35 percentage points across four datasets; dialect-specific results show larger variation, and SIB-200's source-clustered interval includes zero. Paired contrasts with Jev 1.13.0, Gemma-4-31B and Jais-2-8B show a larger Palestinian banking penalty for Jev 1.14.0 than for either LLM under simultaneous uncertainty; the other gap contrasts remain inconclusive. These descriptive findings show why aggregate scores should be read alongside task-family results, coverage and matched language comparisons. They do not establish a general model ranking for dialect robustness or explain the causes of the observed gaps.

title: Constrained Look-ahead Guidance for Interference-Aware Flow Editing
summary: Diffusion and flow models enable powerful generative modeling, but controlled editing remains challenging due to the need to balance source fidelity and edit compliance along the generative trajectory. We propose a principled, inversion-free framework for flow-based image editing from a trajectory centric perspective. Rather than relying on inversion or heuristic guidance, we introduce a one-step look-ahead mechanism that evaluates the effect of candidate updates on both edit and fidelity rewards estimated via denoising, and adjusts the current update based on this evaluation. At each step, our method applies reward-driven corrections guided by the look-ahead evaluation under an explicit fidelity constraint, resulting in stable and coherent trajectory evolution. This look-ahead design mitigates gradient interference between edit and fidelity objectives by anticipating their interaction in future states, leading to improved trade-offs. Experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves stronger semantic edits while better preserving source content compared to existing strong baselines.

title: CompAIssionate Other: Identity Assumptions in LLM Responses to Distress
summary: Individuals experiencing suicidal ideation (SI) or psychological distress may disclose their social identities when seeking support from LLMs. Attending to identity-related stressors can be important for providing contextually appropriate and empathetic support. However, disclosing an identity does not necessarily mean that it is a cause of distress. In this work, we audit how LLMs interpret distress through disclosed identities. Using paired counterfactual interventions, we evaluate six LLMs across two SI and distress datasets, 16 identity and control conditions, and two prompting protocols. Our findings suggest that models can transform identity disclosures into explanatory narratives, attributing distress to presumed identity-related adversity. These assumptions frequently appear within otherwise empathetic responses, particularly when marginalized identities are disclosed. We contextualize our findings through the lens of compassionate othering to characterize these patterns as a form of harm in which empathetic responses impose identity-linked assumptions on individual suffering. These responses can misrepresent individuals' experiences by treating their identities as explanations for distress without supporting evidence. Our findings highlight the need to mitigate these harms by grounding interpretations of distress in individuals' disclosures and avoiding unsupported identity-linked assumptions.

title: Selective Cooperative Perception via Blind Spot Reasoning and Agentic Dialogue with Vision-Language Models
summary: Real-time cooperative perception (CP) in multi-agent traffic environments is highly resource-intensive, which posing scalability challenges for large-scale deployment. Efficiency can be significantly improved by selectively performing CP only in safety-critical scenarios and for key occluding objects. Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are well-suited for complex reasoning in dynamic and uncertain environments, making them a promising tool for this selective CP task. This study proposes a VLM-driven agentic framework for blind spot reasoning and dialogue-based CP. A mixed-model architecture is designed that integrates conventional object detection for stable perception, vision-language reasoning for identifying impactful occlusions, and a physics-based geometric module to align reasoning with real-world visibility constraints. The framework also incorporates a Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting mechanism to enhance interpretability and intent-aware decision-making. We collect real-world data from connected vehicles operating in urban traffic and compare the driving-critical blind spot identification and dialogue performance of four state-of-the-art VLMs. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves over 80% accuracy in driving-critical blind spot detection and over 90% success in dialogue-driven perception sharing. This work provides a scalable, interpretable, and bandwidth-efficient alternative to conventional CP pipelines, and offers new insights into agentic communication design for future connected traffic systems.

summary: Real-time cooperative perception (CP) in multi-agent traffic environments is highly resource-intensive, which posing scalability challenges for large-scale deployment. title: Simple Test-Time Refinement for Plot-to-Code Generation via Visual-Code Diagnostics
summary: Plot-to-code generation has been greatly advanced by recent multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, existing studies mainly focus on one-pass generation or iterative sampling guided by verifier-based filtering, which does not align with the typical human programming workflow of generate first, then iteratively error-location and fix. This naturally motivates a test-time refinement paradigm for plot-to-code generation. In this work, we present the first study on plot-to-code generation via iterative test-time refinement. We propose a Visual-Code Diagnostics framework that enables refinement through visual feedback from source code. Specifically, we first categorize generation errors into four coarse-grained types, and then train lightweight discriminators to recognize and localize these errors based on the rendered visual outputs and corresponding code. Unlike traditional compiler- or debugger-based verification, our approach performs iterative refinement guided by one diagnostics system, enabling more effective semantic and visual correction during test time. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method consistently improves generation quality across diverse generators and significantly outperforms strong test-time scaling baselines.

title: Learning Biological Hierarchies in Single-Cell Foundation Models
summary: Cell types are organized by taxonomic relationships that define lineages in the so-called cell ontology. However, most existing foundation models typically ignore cell-type lineages encoded in this cell ontology. We introduce a biologically informed foundation model called scOntoFM, which embeds hierarchical cell ontology into representation learning. Using Lowest Common Ancestor (LCA) distances from the ontology graph, our framework pairs efficient offline triplet sampling with hierarchical cell-ontology learning. This approach jointly preserves local neighborhoods and shapes the global embedding geometry to reflect the ontology structure. Across diverse cell- and gene-level benchmarks, the model consistently improves performance, with especially strong gains in zero-shot settings. Our model also balances batch integration with biological structure preservation, providing complementary perspectives to existing embedding evaluation frameworks and supporting scalable biological discovery.

title: Elastic Representations via Hyperbolic Geometry
summary: Learned representations (or embeddings) are the foundation of modern machine learning systems, yet they are typically trained as fixed-size embeddings, without accounting for varying downstream resource or task constraints. Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL) addresses this limitation by learning nested representations, but requires costly end-to-end retraining and does not support post hoc expansion, while Contrastive Sparse Representations (CSR) reduce training overhead via lightweight adaptors but operate at a 4x larger dimensionality. Additionally, all prior works restrict their framework towards compression only. In this work, we introduce Hyperbolic Elastic Representation Learning (HERL), a framework for learning dimension-adaptive embeddings (compression and expansion) through a lightweight adaptor without retraining the base encoder. Our key idea is to exploit the exponential capacity of hyperbolic geometry by learning a non-linear mapping from the encoder space to hyperbolic space. We train a simple MLP to downsample the representations before projecting them onto a Lorentzian and learn adaptive representations that respect the Lorentzian geometry. Our approach is model-agnostic and effective in both supervised and unsupervised settings. Through extensive experiments across image and text modalities, we show that HERL preserves downstream performance across a wide range of embedding sizes, exhibits smooth interpolation between dimensions, and achieves these benefits at a fraction of the computational cost. Code: https://github.com/arjunrkaushik/herl.

title: Fine-resolution land-use segmentation and synthetic image-label augmentation in the Kathmandu Valley
summary: Parcel-scale land-use data is missing for most rapidly urbanizing Global South cities, as current segmentation architectures rely on multispectral imagery and planned layouts. We introduce a hand-annotated six-class land-use corpus covering 202 km$^2$ of Kathmandu Valley across 408 fine-resolution RGB scenes. The dataset is uniquely challenging: RGB spectral similarity is high, class imbalance approaches 100:1, and key structural features like rivers measure just two to three pixels wide at a standard hierarchical decoder's prediction stride. Evaluating five architectures reveals that standard random data splitting conceals massive spatial leakage. Switching to a strict sequence-block split drops performance by up to 0.095 mIoU. This penalty exceeds the performance gap between the architectures themselves. We modified the SegFormer baseline by integrating a half-resolution residual detail path, boundary-reliability reweighting, a topology-aware loss, and a presence-balanced sampler. Adding only 1.9% more parameters, the enhanced architecture improves mean IoU across every test fold, with gains concentrated in rare, thin-structure classes. However, both models achieve identical results on the external LoveDA benchmark. Finally, augmenting with diffusion-generated pairs at matched compute degraded accuracy across all architectures, especially harming rare classes it aimed to improve. This demonstrates that blindly incorporating synthetic data can severely damage performance, highlighting a critical need to rigorously evaluate and filter generated samples before training.

title: HARP-Bench: Benchmarking Robot Manipulation Around Active Humans
summary: Recent robot manipulation benchmarks have enabled systematic evaluation of general-purpose robot policies across diverse objects, scenes, instructions, and embodiments. However, most existing benchmarks still assume that the robot is the only active agent and that task semantics are determined primarily by the instruction and object state. This assumption overlooks a common source of real-world variation: humans actively sharing the workspace. In such settings, humans may reveal an implicit goal, complete part of the task, temporarily change object availability, or constrain safe robot motion while working nearby. We introduce HARP-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating robot manipulation policies in workspaces shared with active humans. HARP-Bench treats human activity as part of the manipulation problem, rather than as background scene variation. It organizes human-present manipulation into four conditions: Cueing, Contribution, Interruption, and Co-presence. These conditions are instantiated through everyday manipulation tasks, including paired human-present variants for controlled comparison with standard manipulation. HARP-Bench also provides a demonstration-generation pipeline for dynamic human-present settings. We evaluate VLA models, imitation-learning methods, and heuristic policies on HARP-Bench. Human-present variations challenge current policies, and higher task success does not consistently improve safety. Quantitative failure analysis identifies manipulation and recovery as the dominant remaining challenges. Training with HARP-Bench demonstrations improves human-present performance in simulation. A real-world study on one task family shows improved performance under human contribution, but not interruption, providing initial evidence of the data's utility and identifying limits of transfer. Code is available at https://github.com/UMass-Embodied-AGI/harp.

title: KeyASRBench: Measuring Whole-Phrase Keyword Preservation in Real-World ASR
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, 4 tables. Bilingual ASR evaluation with a 10-hour model-conditioned challenge set and a disjoint 30-minute model-blind control
summary: Public automatic speech recognition (ASR) benchmarks increasingly report low sequence error rates, yet production systems still use hotword lists, contextual biasing, retrieval, and post-correction. This motivates a complementary question: does a transcript preserve selected names, products, technical terms, versions, and relational phrases? We present KeyASRBench, a bilingual pilot that operationalizes occurrence-based Keyword Error Rate (KER) over frozen whole-phrase annotations. The 10-hour model-conditioned challenge set contains 1,501 Chinese and English clips with 4,723 keyword occurrences. Across five locally inferred checkpoints and two official API systems, language-specific MER/WER ranges from 5.31% to 12.91%, while KER ranges from 13.61% to 33.81%. A disjoint 30-minute model-blind control yields KER of 10.65%-27.31%. The control confirms that selected-phrase errors extend beyond challenge-set selection.

title: Confidence-driven adaptive semantic transmission for task-oriented communication
summary: Image-based remote monitoring over wireless networks faces a trade-off between communication cost and classification reliability. Transmitting complete images is communication-intensive, whereas relying solely on lightweight edge classifiers may compromise accuracy. To address this challenge, we propose Confidence-Driven Adaptation (CDA) for image transmission and classification. An edge device (ED) captures images and applies a lightweight classifier before transmission to a remote server. Based on its classification confidence, the ED selects among three transmission modes with varying levels of information: a short text string reporting its predicted class when confidence is high, a compressed Region of Interest (ROI) at intermediate confidence levels, or an uncompressed ROI when confidence is low. The server accepts the predicted class directly in the first case and performs classification using a more powerful classifier in the other two cases. Numerical evaluations under bandwidth-limited, lossy links and latency-constrained settings demonstrate that CDA achieves high task accuracy at the receiver compared with non-adaptive baselines that transmit only the edge-classifier outcome or the uncompressed ROI.

title: A Geometry-Guided Feature-Space Framework for Interpretable Unsupervised 4D-STEM Analysis of Complex Multiphase Materials
summary: Rapid, high-fidelity analysis of four-dimensional scanning transmission electron microscopy (4D-STEM) datasets from heterogeneous materials remains challenging because coexisting phases, orientation variants, local strain gradients, and intrinsic TEM thin-foil effects produce complex, overlapping diffraction signatures. Here, we present a machine-learning (ML) framework that combines physics-informed geometric descriptors with weighted high-dimensional embeddings to identify latent structural patterns with minimal prior knowledge. By constructing a regularized descriptor space before embedding and density-based clustering, the method improves cluster stability, suppresses noise-driven fragmentation, and reduces sensitivity to embedding hyperparameters. Spatial weighting produced the largest stability gain, increasing median cluster persistence from 0.04 to 0.55 while reducing the noise fraction from approximately 22% to 0%. Rotation weighting increased DBCV from 0.80 to 0.92, although the noise fraction rose from 0.2% to 1.0%, highlighting a trade-off between improved density separation and noise rejection. We validate the framework on two benchmark systems: Si/Si$_x$Ge$_{1-x}$ epitaxial layers with continuous lattice variation and deformation, and multiphase Ti-Nb alloys containing distinct phases and orientation variants. Comparisons with a pretrained vanilla autoencoder and model-free pattern vectorization show that the physics-informed geometric descriptor provides higher cluster fidelity, greater interpretability, and substantially lower dimensionality.

title: Full Fine-Tuning is not the Problem: Why Adam Fails and SGD Succeeds in Few-Shot CLIP Adaptation
summary: Few-shot CLIP adaptation is often treated as a parameterization problem. Full fine-tuning is assumed to overfit, so parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods are preferred. In this paper, we show that this conclusion conflates parameterization with optimization. Across 11 datasets, 3 CLIP backbones, and 5 shot levels, dense full fine-tuning with plain SGD outperforms representative PEFT methods under the reported evaluation protocol, whereas Adam/AdamW collapses. We trace this collapse to unreliable support-set preconditioning. The few-shot second moment systematically underestimates the corresponding full-data statistic, already at initialization. Adam's inverse-square-root normalization converts this error into an oversized adaptive update. Matching Adam's first-step update budget to SGD resolves most of the collapse, whereas numerator-side alignment does not explain the failure. Shampoo and SOAP also fail, so richer preconditioning alone does not resolve the problem. Theory formalizes how few-shot estimation error is amplified into unsafe updates. SGD succeeds because it avoids unreliable preconditioners and stays close to pretrained CLIP. Interpolation probes show low-loss connections along tested directions, and curvature probes show favorable directional curvature. These results identify optimizer-induced preconditioning, not dense full fine-tuning itself, as the main source of failure in few-shot CLIP adaptation.

title: Self-contained Data Cleaning for Unsupervised Anomaly Detection
summary: Training datasets for unsupervised anomaly detection are often assumed to be anomaly-free, but in practice, they frequently contain malicious or anomalous contamination. This contamination severely degrades the dependability and security of downstream detection models. While some contamination-robust methods exist, they rarely generalize across different model architectures and typically rely on a priori knowledge of the contamination ratio\textemdash information that is rarely available in real-world security operations. In this paper, we propose a novel, self-contained preprocessing framework for anomaly detection that identifies and removes training set contamination without relying on known contamination ratios. Our approach performs a dynamic analysis of the cosine similarity between each data point and its reconstruction during the early training stages of an auto-encoder, mapping points into a dynamic space where anomalous regions naturally exhibit lower density. By executing ``hard cleaning''\textemdash removing all identified anomalous candidates from the training pool\textemdash we systematically improve data quality. Because this cleaning occurs at the data level, the security and reliability improvements generalize seamlessly across various downstream anomaly detection architectures. Evaluating our framework across 8 distinct models and 10 security-relevant datasets, our approach achieves up to 100\% contamination reduction, yielding average improvements of 11.2\% in F1 score and 7.3\% in classification accuracy.

title: Edge Computing for Computer Vision in IoT: Feasibility and Directions
summary: The convergence of decentralized architectures integrating Machine Learning, Computer Vision and Low Power Wide Area Networks is increasingly becoming an integral part of our daily existence. Internet of Things serves as a real-time data conduit enhancing decision making via embedded technology and continuous data exchange. This paper explores the feasibility of Edge Computing as a foundational pillar in this evolving landscape. We experiment under real world, dynamic conditions, evaluate the technological aspects, strategies, process flows and key observations under the broad Edge Computing domain. Research pathways include Multi-access Edge topologies in future 6G networks, model quantization, and satellite-enhanced communication platforms. Additionally, a discussion is added supporting the advanced AI functionalities, including zero-shot learning, multi modal perception, and decentralized generative AI, thereby broadening the scope of intelligent applications across various domains. The significance and research objective of this study are threefold: (1) evaluation of LoRaWAN and satellite IoT communication strategies, (2) analysis of CV workloads on edge hardware and (3) future research directions where Edge Computing can support low-latency, energy-efficient and socially impactful IoT applications. By explicitly addressing these aspects, we aim to establish a clear link between the technological feasibility, ultimately with a practical and socioeconomic relevance.

title: Structurally Separated DAG Learning with Multi-Scale Normalized Closure
summary: Continuous DAG learning commonly enforces acyclicity through scalar functions of a weighted adjacency that aggregate evidence from weighted closed walks. We add a complementary layer: matrix-valued closure logits---explicit multi-hop structural relation scores for each ordered pair---supervised alongside data fit, sparsity, and a DAGMA-style barrier on the weighted adjacency. The distinction is not scalarization of the overall objective but how path evidence is represented and exposed before aggregation. SMNC (scale-normalized multi-scale closure) builds these scores on a structural gate by repeated squaring in log space and divides each scale by its path-length budget, counteracting product-style attenuation along long cycles; diagonal entries support node-wise cycle supervision and off-diagonals optional pairwise reachability cues. In the linear model, a bounded structure--magnitude factorization ties strong effective edges to strong gates; a nonlinear induced gate offers another construction with the same intent. For sufficiently strong cycles, normalized logits admit a length-independent lower bound; under a unique-active-cycle assumption, the hard final-scale readout yields a polynomial log-gate gradient factor rather than exponential product-style decay. On cue-free, unstandardized Gaussian linear and nonlinear ER benchmarks, these models improve over DAGMA, run with default hyperparameters at a reduced budget, on denser graphs and are close to it on sparse ones.

title: Chatter Attack: Resource Consumption Attack for Large Language Models
summary: LLMs are powerful but incur substantial inference cost, which can be exploited by malicious users to induce overly long outputs, increasing latency and operational expense. Prior resource consumption attacks either coerce repetition or suppress the end-of-sequence token by lowering its logit value. However, with autoregressive, sampling-based generation, the search space grows exponentially with length and small deviations or unstable trajectories can derail optimization, limiting attack effectiveness and stability. To address this issue, we introduce Chatter Attack, a novel class of resource consumption attacks that optimize adversarial prompts to induce predefined short target phrases, thereby avoiding search-space explosion while still eliciting long responses. Specifically, Chatter Attack triggers self-doubt using short doubt-inducing phrases as the target, and sustains this state throughout generation via inference attention loss and global entropy loss. To extend to black-box settings, we further propose a novel Bayesian Prompt Optimization (BPO) method, which models the objective function globally by constructing a discrete token kernel, efficiently exploring the entire search space using prior information. Extensive experiments across multiple models and datasets show that our method outperforms baselines, with maximum response length increases to 31.5$\times$, and revealing practical resource-depletion risks for real-world LLM inference services.

title: Interactive Person Retrieval with On-the-Fly Visual Feedback
summary: Traditional text-based person retrieval (TPR) assumes that a witness provides a complete description at once, whereas interactive person retrieval (Inter-PR) refines a partial description through question-answer exchanges. In this setting, the questioner inspects retrieved candidates to decide what evidence to request next, while the answerer sees only the witness-side memory and cannot report candidate-specific visual differences. Existing methods mainly learn offline question orderings, leaving this visual-feedback loop underexplored. To address this limitation, we introduce visual-feedback interactive person retrieval (VFI-PR), a new interactive retrieval paradigm in which retrieved candidates produce visual feedback that becomes evidence for subsequent questioning and re-ranking. To support training and evaluation in this setting, we construct VFI-PEDES, a dataset and evaluation protocol for visual-feedback interaction, and propose VFI-ReID, a framework that learns to use visual feedback during interactive person retrieval. Through the Dynamic Accumulated-evidence Retriever (DAR) and retrieval-aware question optimization, VFI-ReID adapts retrieval and question generation to evolving evidence states, turning visual feedback into complementary evidence for subsequent retrieval. Experiments show that VFI-ReID consistently improves retrieval across VFI-PR interaction stages, demonstrating the utility of visual feedback for interactive person retrieval and outperforming existing Inter-PR baselines.

title: A Unified Framework for License Plate Identification and Character-Recognition
summary: This paper presents a unified framework for license plate detection and character recognition on low-power edge hardware. The proposed network uses a shared CSP-Darknet and PANet feature encoder with an anchor-free localization head and a RoIAlign-based sequence-recognition branch. Character decoding is performed directly on aligned feature maps, avoiding image-space plate cropping and a second recognition backbone. The model is trained on an AI-assisted dataset of approximately 37,000 manually verified images covering license plate layouts from all 50 United States. The dataset includes variations in illumination, viewpoint, weather, blur, occlusion, and plate design. The framework is converted to an INT8 TensorRT engine and evaluated on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano with 8 GB memory. The INT8 model shows an mAP50 of 97.8% and a full-sequence accuracy of 90.7%. It records 147 FPS at 6.8 ms end-to-end latency, with 315 MB inference memory and 9.4 W average power consumption. Relative to the YOLOv8s+CRNN baseline, the proposed deployment provides a 7.1x throughput increase and a 77.8% reduction in allocated inference memory

title: Zero-Shot VLA Adaptation with Retrieved Guidance
summary: Pre-training large parametric "Vision-Language-Action" (VLA) models on large demonstration datasets has recently yielded promising results for general-purpose manipulation. However, these models still struggle under even small domain shifts relative to the training data, such as changes in camera viewpoint, background, object identity, or robot morphology. Motivated by the success of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) in language models, we pursue retrieval to boost VLA performance. Specifically, we seek to leverage retrieval from domain-mismatched, "in-the-wild" demonstration datasets like DROID to guide a VLA's behavior in a new target domain. To achieve this, we introduce RAGu, which overcomes robotics-specific challenges for RAG: (1) It incorporates simple geometric calibration to transform source demonstrations into the target setup and reduce cross-domain differences. (2) It uses a coarse-to-fine retrieval strategy that selects, from a large pool of pre-warped candidates, the trajectory most compatible with the base VLA. (3) It guides the VLA's flow-matching inference procedure rather than seeking to retrain the base model or expand its limited context window. We evaluate RAGu across real-world, simulation, sim-to-real transfer, and cross-embodiment humanoid manipulation. We find it improves real-world VLA success rates from 20% to 80% and outperforms the closest-related baselines in sim. Project website: raguvla.github.io

title: Multi-Node Transformers for Object Detection and Captioning Across Distributed Edge Networks
summary: This paper presents a unified transformer-based framework for object detection and dense region captioning across distributed edge networks. The architecture uses a shared visual encoder followed by detection, region extraction, and autoregressive language-decoding stages, allowing localization and region description to reuse the same image features. This design removes the second image-encoding path required by decoupled detection and captioning pipelines. To support execution on resource-limited devices, a workload-allocation formulation assigns model stages and input streams across connected edge nodes while accounting for execution time, memory capacity, processor utilization, power limits, and intermediate tensor transfer cost. The framework is evaluated on a six-device edge testbed comprising four NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano and Orin NX inference nodes and two Raspberry Pi 5 auxiliary CPU nodes, with TensorRT FP16 and INT8 execution on the NVIDIA devices. On a Jetson Orin Nano, the unified INT8 model achieves 38.1 FPS with 3.5 GB peak memory use and 11.8 W measured power. Under four concurrent streams, the proposed allocation achieves 35.2 FPS and 28.4 ms mean end-to-end latency with an internode transfer rate of 6.8 MB/s.

title: Robust Satisficing Ensemble: Scalable Model Aggregation Under Distribution Shifts
summary: Standard ensemble methods can improve robustness by mitigating individual model stochasticity, but they frequently fail to generalize beyond the training distribution, leaving systems vulnerable to out-of-distribution (OOD) data. We introduce the Robust Satisficing Ensemble (RSE), a scalable probabilistic aggregation framework designed to secure model combinations by minimizing their fragility against distributional changes. By bridging a robust satisficing objective with a quadratic risk surrogate, RSE derives an analytical inner adversary. This fundamental reformulation enables highly efficient weight updates without the computational bottleneck of standard minimax optimization, crucially decoupling optimization complexity from sample size to scale effectively to large datasets. In particular, we prove a geometrically decaying truncation error for the fragility approximation via Lagrange-Burmann expansion and establish stationarity guarantees for RSE. We evaluate RSE across a comprehensive spectrum of distribution shifts, including adversarial label shift (SST-5, TREC), natural subpopulation and temporal shifts (CivilComments, HuffPost). Our results demonstrate that RSE consistently outperforms strong robust baselines, including GroupDRO, IRM, and SRM. These findings establish RSE as a practical, theoretically grounded safeguard for reliable model aggregation in dynamic environments.

title: Single-Radar Bilateral 3D Near-Field Imaging for Mobile Robots
summary: Mobile robots operating in homes need reliable 3D perception of nearby furniture and surrounding structures, yet recovering this information on both sides of the robot's path with a single forward-mounted millimeter-wave radar remains challenging because of near-field wavefront curvature, viewpoint-dependent target visibility, and limited elevation diversity. This paper presents a motion-assisted framework for reconstructing structures on both sides of a robot's trajectory. Our near-field model relates scene reflectivity to stepped-frequency multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) observations across frequencies and robot positions using spherical paths from transmitter (Tx) to scatterer to receiver (Rx). Bilateral Tx combining provides wideband directional weighting, while sliding-aperture back-projection coherently focuses the measurements using near-field propagation distances. Top-K power fusion combines local images with different visibility. The reconstruction provides lateral-forward support for multi-layer height extraction, followed by guarded adaptive height refinement using the original MIMO channels. Experiments in controlled, office/study, and corridor environments produce mean lateral-forward localization errors of 4.65, 5.63, and 5.98 cm, respectively, with peak-to-background ratios (PBRs) exceeding 13 dB. The framework recovers bilateral 3D scattering structure from one forward pass using a single radar, without relying on learned representations of the scene.

title: DeepFinance: Can AI Diligence a $100MM Deal?
summary: Existing evaluations of AI models on high-finance work focus on retrieving answers from financial documents and producing numerically correct outputs. Real private equity (PE) and investment banking (IB) work also depends on choosing between conflicting sources, making sound assumptions, and keeping every step auditable. We introduce DeepFinance, an ultra long-horizon benchmark of 21 end-to-end PE and IB tasks that take a human professional an average of 27.1 hours. Each task pairs a request with a data room averaging 19 files and is graded against an average of 84 expert-written rubric criteria covering output, workflow, and judgment. We evaluate 22 model configurations, each in its native agent harness. The best configuration, GPT-6 Astra with max reasoning, satisfies 57.6% of rubric criteria, and the top four configurations are not statistically distinguishable. Frontier models often calculate correctly from the wrong inputs and find decision-relevant evidence without acting on it.

title: Decomposing Earth Embeddings with Sparse Autoencoders
summary: Earth observation foundation models produce global metre-resolution embeddings that underpin work across agriculture, ecology, hydrology, and beyond. Yet these embeddings are opaque: each dimension entangles unrelated physical concepts, which makes them difficult to interpret and their robustness hard to assess. Here, we propose sparse autoencoders (SAEs) as a principled way to decompose Earth embeddings into sparse, approximately monosemantic features over an overcomplete dictionary. Because LLM judges of interpretations do not transfer to satellite pixels, and spatial autocorrelation matters, we introduce a tailored evaluation protocol. It scores any SAE on reconstruction at matched sparsity, alignment with reference concepts, and spatial scale, each against baselines that include an SAE whose decoder is a frozen random dictionary. On this protocol, SAEs reconstruct AlphaEarth and Tessera embeddings better than every baseline at matched sparsity. Their features align with far fewer reference concepts than raw embedding dimensions (on AlphaEarth, 88% align with at most one of 20 concept groups, most with none, against a median of 12 per raw dimension). They also carry more of their variance at fine spatial scales (23 to 32% within a 640 m patch for BatchTopK and Matryoshka, against 9%). An SAE with a frozen random decoder shares both properties, which therefore follow from sparsity, whereas only a learned dictionary reconstructs the embedding accurately: on AlphaEarth, trained SAEs leave eight times less variance unexplained. We test the sparse code on two applications, discovering land-cover sub-concepts and detecting out-of-distribution pixels by area-of-applicability estimation. Both indicate how sparse features could be used, but neither is yet reliable enough for practical use. Together, these results are a step toward Earth observation models whose features can be inspected.

title: Semantic Synthesis over Brute-Force Search: LLM-Guided Transformation Design for Efficient Learning
summary: Data transformation pipelines shape the training distribution in computer vision, but designing them is a computationally expensive problem. We investigate whether large language models can enable efficient discovery by synthesizing executable transformation programs outside predefined augmentation spaces. We compare nine strategies under a unified training protocol, including standard augmentation policies, brute-force search, direct code generation with two LLMs, and performance-guided generation using LLMs fine-tuned on accuracy-ordered transformation pairs. When the best candidates are retrained for 20 epochs, LLM-generated transformation programs lead on every dataset, reaching 0.8877 accuracy on CIFAR-10, 0.5825 on CIFAR-100, and 0.9588 on SVHN, surpassing brute-force search over 6,000 candidates. The best transform on CIFAR-10 and SVHN comes from a fine-tuned generator using 270 candidates, while the best on CIFAR-100 comes from an off-the-shelf generator using only 10. This needs 22x fewer candidate evaluations in the generation step and 600x fewer for off-the-shelf generations, relative to brute-force search. Beyond transformation discovery, we analyze the reliability of the reduced-budget evaluation commonly used for augmentation search. Correlating one-epoch selection scores with 20-epoch outcomes reveals strong, weak, and absent predictive relationships depending on the dataset and architecture, with correlations ranging from 0.756 to near zero. A positive control indicates that range restriction alone is unlikely to explain the low correlations. Our results indicate that semantic synthesis with code LLMs provides an efficient alternative to search-based transformation discovery and highlight the importance of validating evaluation fidelity when optimizing data transformations.

title: Off-Policy RL with Online Inference Tuning: My Solution to the CoRL 2026 RoboEval Challenge
comment: Technical report for the RoboEval Challenge at CoRL 2026. Code: https://github.com/IliaLarchenko/RoboEvalSolution ; checkpoint: https://huggingface.co/IliaLarchenko/RoboEvalSolution ; project page: https://ilialarchenko.com/projects/roboeval2026/
summary: The CoRL 2026 RoboEval challenge has eight bimanual tasks, and it ranks a policy not only on whether it succeeds but on how: every stage of the task, done safely, efficiently and with both arms in coordination, scored against human demonstrations. My solution has two parts. The generic part, carried over from my LeHome challenge solution, is off-policy RL on a $π_{0.5}$-based policy that is also its own value function. It is trained with AWR and RECAP on advantages of the exact official score, in a loop where every rollout is at the same time a Thompson-sampling trial of about 20 inference parameters. Out of the box, it took the policy to 0.85 RDS on held-out seeds in two days (and it was still very far from convergence). The competition-specific part adds data that local exploration cannot find: generated demonstrations that reach the full reward, and recovery episodes that start from the policy's own failures. The submitted policy reaches 0.990 RDS on held-out seeds and 0.987 on the official seeds.

title: CoupledFlow: One-Step Neural Operators for Coupled Multi-Physics PDEs
summary: This paper introduces COUPLED FLOW, a new neural operator learning framework for multi-physics PDE systems that captures the co-evolution of multiple physical processes by modeling their cross-process interactions. Unlike existing neural operator methods that primarily target single-physics settings, COUPLED FLOW employs a novel structure-constrained flow matching algorithm to learn process- specific mean velocity fields conditioned on the full multi-physics state. This enables fast and accurate one-step prediction of coupled PDE systems that would otherwise require expensive numerical simulations. A key challenge in training COUPLED FLOW however lies in sampling structure-constrained conditional flow interpolants that capture cross-process correlations and serve as training examples for flow matching. To address this challenge, we derive a multi-physics mean-flow consistency identity that characterizes cross-process interactions and defines the structure-constrained mean-flow matching loss. To provide informative training samples for flow matching with this loss, we develop a principled method for sampling correlated conditional interpolants based on posterior multi-output Gaus- sian processes, which capture richer cross-process correlations than the commonly used endpoint-conditioned linear interpolants. We also establish a theoretical re- sult showing that the Wasserstein-2 distance between the predicted and oracle PDE solution distributions is upper-bounded in terms of the structure-constrained flow matching loss and the smoothness of the learned flow. Experiments across diverse coupled PDE benchmarks demonstrate that COUPLED FLOW consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art neural operators and generative PDE solvers.

title: Kimodo-Policy: Learning Kinematic Action Models for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
comment: 23 pages, 14 figures, 4 tables. Project page: https://kimodo-policy.github.io/
summary: Humanoid loco-manipulation requires continuous coordination of high-dimensional whole-body motion to realize task objectives. While vision-language-action models and world action models transfer semantic and visual-dynamics priors to robot control, these priors do not necessarily capture the structure of robot motion. We introduce Kinematic Action Models (KAMs), a paradigm that treats whole-body motion as a direct pretraining target and uses a pretrained motion generator as the primary action-generation backbone. KAMs ground learned temporal and cross-body coordination priors through task conditioning, visual observations, and execution feedback. We present Kimodo-Policy as an initial instantiation, combining a frozen Kimodo text-to-motion backbone with lightweight ControlNet-based visual conditioning. A root-body-hand hierarchy coordinates locomotion and manipulation, while motion-history conditioning and repeated action-chunk prediction bridge motion synthesis and closed-loop control. Following large-scale loco-manipulation pretraining, the policy achieves the highest overall success among compared policies on multi-task HumanoidArena (72.14%), competitive performance on SIMPLE, and 60% mean success across eight real-world tasks, with 678M parameters (92M trainable). Ablations support the contribution of the pretrained motion backbone. Together, these results provide initial evidence for motion generation as a complementary foundation for humanoid action learning.

title: Interpretable Cyber-Physical Attack Detection in Smart Grids: A Leakage-Controlled Multi-Testbed Evaluation of Fusion, Robustness, and Observability Limits
summary: Cyber-physical smart-grid detectors are typically treated as black boxes and validated exclusively on clean, temporally shuffled datasets, which risk overly optimistic performance claims. This work presents a multi-testbed evaluation study built around an interpretable, time-windowed fusion Random Forest, adopting the pessimistic result whenever evaluation protocols disagree. (i) On a public paired cyber-physical dataset, shuffled cross-validation is optimistic: macro-F1 falls from 0.96 to 0.88 +/- 0.06 under rolling-origin temporal evaluation. A topology-free graph convolutional network (GCN) serving as a control confirms that this lightweight model is competitive on these splits. (ii) The adaptive and adaptive-joint feature-space attacks, which are infeasible as realistic grid manipulations, degrade macro-F1 to 0.67 and 0.34, respectively. Adversarial training and randomized smoothing partially restore performance, and a physics-constrained evolution-strategy evasion on the IEEE 14-Bus testbed shows the same vulnerability pattern. (iii) On real IEC-104 traffic, the cyber view reliably catches structural attacks (recall of 0.87 to 0.98) but largely fails on semantic value manipulation (recall of 0.11 to 0.35). An observability taxonomy on the IEEE 14-Bus system reveals that stealthy false data injection defeats all three observation views. (iv) On a full AC weighted least-squares state-estimation testbed, a forecasting-aided temporal test is evaded by slow ramps precisely where a rate-invariant physics-manifold test sustains detection at a common 5% false-alarm target. A full end-to-end evaluation on IEEE 118-Bus confirms the ordering but bounds its strength: the manifold test detects every trial down to 0.05 degree/step and 0.48 at 0.02 degree/step, against 0.14 for the temporal test. All code and benchmarks are released.

title: Feel My Focus: Gaze-Triggered Digital Twin Creation for Remote Collaboration
summary: We present Feel My Focus, a gaze-triggered mixed reality (MR) demonstration that enables rapid creation and sharing of lightweight 3D digital twins during remote collaboration. Unlike systems that use gaze primarily as a referential pointer, Feel My Focus treats sustained visual attention as a generative action: a fixation on a physical object initiates single-image capture, attention-guided segmentation, and one-shot 3D reconstruction, allowing a remote partner to inspect and discuss the object in situ. The system integrates gaze-tracking glasses, modular segmentation and reconstruction services, and an MR client for runtime streaming and interaction. This design prioritizes responsiveness and experiential continuity over photometric fidelity. We report observations from a public demonstration, highlighting design trade-offs, failure modes, and user control considerations for deploying gaze-triggered generative systems in real-world collaborative settings.

title: Hybrid Source Code Change Impact Analysis
summary: Change impact analysis (CIA) helps developers identify code entities impacted by their initial changes. While several approaches for CIA were proposed, they still struggle with either low precision or low recall, thereby increasing manual effort for developers to verify the results. Furthermore, limitations in the used datasets and experimental setups can bias the results reported by many CIA approaches. In this paper, we first address the dataset limitations by manually labeling 1,931 changed code entities stemming from 263 commits of 22 open-source Java projects. Next, we introduce two variants of katIA, our code change impact analysis approach that combines static impact analysis with the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs). The first variant uses a single prompt (katIA-SP) for refining an initial static impact set while the second variant uses three specialized agents (katIA-MA). The evaluation with our curated dataset shows that katIA-SP with Gemini 2.5 Flash achieved an F1-score of 22.4% when matching impacted entities by their fully qualified names (FQN) and 27.0% when matching them by their class and entity names (CE). The latter shows an improvement of 2.0 percentage points over the state-of-the-art. This score is further improved by katIA-MA which, using Gemini 2.5 Flash, yields an FQN-matching F1-score of 29.1% and a CE-matching F1-score of 33.3%. While these improvements come at the cost of increased median generation time from 0.570 s to 11.214 s and median token usage from 1,235 to 6,462 tokens, the improved performance justifies the additional cost. The comparison of three LLMs using katIA-SP finds that Gemini 2.5 Flash is the most consistent model. These results indicate that combining static impact analysis with LLM-based refinement, particularly with the multi-agent variant, can improve code change impact analysis.

title: Budget-aware Correspondence-driven View Selection for Real-time 3D Perception of Mobile Robots
summary: 3D visual perception and scene reconstruction are critical for autonomous robots and intelligent transportation, yet real-world deployments often generate long, redundant image sequences that hinder downstream processing. This report investigates BCVS (budget-aware correspondence-driven view sampling), a pose-free view selection algorithm that offers 22+ FPS on a CPU, enabling online filtering for efficient 3D perception by mobile robots. Unlike existing approaches that rely on full structure-from-motion (SfM) pipelines or camera pose estimation, BCVS employs a purely correspondence-based scoring strategy that prioritizes view novelty while maintaining sufficient overlap for geometric stability. Given a user-specified budget, BCVS iteratively selects the most distinct frames and suppresses near-duplicates, producing compact subsets that preserve connectivity and minimize reconstruction loss. Extensive experiments on benchmark show that BCVS outperforms CPU-friendly baselines at tight budgets and remains competitive as budgets scale. Field trials with large aerial and marine robotics data further validate its practicality and scalability: BCVS reduces redundancy up to 16% while sustaining robust SfM registration and high-quality 3D reconstructions.

title: Anatomy-Activated Mixture-of-Experts for 3D Medical Vision-Language Pre-training
summary: Medical Vision-Language Pre-training (VLP) leverages the semantic richness of radiology reports to learn 3D representations, yet current architectures remain fundamentally anatomy-agnostic. While clinical diagnostics rely on organ-specific context, standard encoders apply a uniform, dense parameterization to all volumetric patches, and existing Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) routers gate on isolated local features without explicit access to the organ composition of the scan or crop. We propose Anatomy-Activated Mixture-of-Experts (A$^{2}$MoE), a framework that incorporates anatomical inductive biases within the model's computational path. A$^{2}$MoE introduces two key components: (1) a Histogram Representation Router (HRR) that conditions expert selection on global visual context and a predicted anatomical composition histogram, encouraging anatomy-dependent expert weighting; and (2) an Organ-Query Multi-Scale Projector (OQMSP) that utilizes learnable queries to extract organ-level embeddings for fine-grained alignment without requiring manual annotations at inference. By routing at the patch level rather than the token level, A$^{2}$MoE reduces routing complexity by orders of magnitude while satisfying load balancing by construction. Pre-trained on over 60,000 multi-phase CT scans, A$^{2}$MoE achieves state-of-the-art performance across segmentation, classification, and detection benchmarks. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our anatomically grounded inductive biases support robust generalization to MRI and ultrasound, establishing a scalable foundation for medical representation learning. The code is available at https://github.com/gmum/A2MoE.

title: How Many Candidates Does a One-Step World Model Need? A Random-Codebook Account of Nearest-of-m Training on Frozen DINO Tokens
comment: 30 pages (12-page main text, appendices A-H). Code: https://github.com/thddydgnl/nearest-of-m-world-models
summary: One-step stochastic world models avoid the mode averaging of deterministic feature predictors without the tens of network evaluations per step that diffusion and flow matching require. The simplest such objective is nearest-of-m matching (conditional implicit maximum likelihood estimation, IMLE): draw m candidate futures and pull only the one closest to the observed outcome. Recent work conjectures that a small m suffices for feature-space world models and that a strictly proper energy score should replace the hard minimum. We test both claims with one-step world models on frozen DINOv2/v3 patch tokens, using benchmarks whose futures can be enumerated. Under mode-like uncertainty, nearest-of-m with m=16 covers the enumerated futures better than 50-step flow matching (at about 1/30 of its latency), one-step flow generators and an energy-score generator at matched parameter counts, and its rollouts stay on the token manifold where flow rollouts drift. One quantity governs the choice of m: the nearest-of-m objective is the expected distortion of a random codebook of m draws from the generator. This view yields three predictions, recorded before the corresponding runs: (i) memorization of the realized outcome in contexts that never repeat, whose strength is governed by the codebook's miss distortion I(m) rather than its miss probability, and which an energy-score generator does not escape by raising m; (ii) a flattening of mode probabilities with m, matching a known optimum within 0.01; and (iii) under-dispersion on continuous high-dimensional outcomes, which bounds the method on real robot video. Per-step matching on self-rollouts cuts long-horizon error by a third on a stochastic Push-T variant; an ablation separates its manifold and coverage benefits. Planning success does not improve despite accurate risk estimates, a negative result we report with its diagnosis.

title: DM-Call: Decision-Model-Guided Function Calling with Cumulative Verification Feedback
summary: Reliable function calling requires Large Language Models (LLMs) to select appropriate functions and generate arguments consistent with user intent. However, syntactically valid calls may still be semantically incorrect due to inappropriate function selection or mismatched arguments. In this paper, we propose Decision-Model-Guided Function Calling (DM-Call), a framework that combines local schema validation with separate decision-model verification of function selection and argument correctness. For rejected candidates, DM-Call accumulates verification probabilities, binary judgments, and schema errors across attempts. A hybrid feedback representation further combines numerical probabilities with verbal correctness labels to guide iterative refinement without executing external tools. Extensive evaluation across BFCL and API-Bank (first-call) demonstrates DM-Call boosts function-calling accuracy versus direct generation, at modest additional cost.

title: Shaping Useful Noise: Energy Distributions Predict Visual Pretraining Quality
comment: Accepted as an oral presentation to NeurIPS 2026 (Sydney)
summary: Synthetic data can scale visual pretraining, but current selection criteria only partially explain which datasets train strong representations. We propose using the energy profile of a dataset--the distribution of log-probability levels it occupies under a normalised real-image density model--as an audit and curation principle for synthetic data. To operationalise this view, we introduce Energy-Level Distribution Distance (ELD), which compares real and synthetic energy distributions. Real images span sparse high-likelihood scenes and dense low-likelihood textures, so useful synthetic data should cover this energy range rather than collapse to likely but low-variation samples. Across diverse synthetic datasets, ELD exposes mismatches missed by FID and predicts pretraining performance beyond FID, LPIPS variation, and feature-space recall, including across CNN and ViT self-supervised settings. We then use ELD to resample and mix synthetic sources, matching the real-image energy histogram while preserving diversity and improving downstream transfer.

title: Think or Remember: The Exchange Rate of Agentic Inference
summary: Agents built on reasoning models resend their growing transcript at every call. Two transacting parties, not the model, decide what that costs: the client keeps or edits messages; the server decides whether earlier reasoning returns in the prompt and what its cache reuses. We define a cost model whose counts match an instrumented engine exactly; the architecture charges $c$ per token processed and $β$ per pair attended. Their ratio $P^*=c/β$ is an exchange rate between thinking and remembering: per token, processing dominates below this context length, a thinking regime, and attention above it, a memory regime. A policy change has a mechanical cost, incurred even if the agent writes the same tokens, and a behavioral one: it writes different tokens, changing cost and outcome. Serving alone can flip which policy is cheaper: on recorded Qwen3-8B ScienceWorld runs, dropping earlier reasoning costs 1.74 times keeping it when the server reuses generated states and 0.34 times when it reuses nothing. In live reruns, dropping it cuts correct HotpotQA answers by 9-23 percentage points on four models, at lower point-estimate cost. Comparing context policies means comparing systems: architecture and serving set the cost of the history kept and the work it induces.

title: MUTE: Multi-Level Alignment Uncoupling Against Talking-Head Exploitation for Voice Protection
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 33 pages, including appendix and checklist. Project and code: https://github.com/jindl465/MUTE
summary: Talking-head generation models, which synthesize realistic facial animations from audio, are increasingly vulnerable to misuse in multimodal deepfake scenarios. Protecting such systems remains challenging, as talking-head models fundamentally rely on precise audio-visual alignment, while effective audio protection methods remain largely underexplored. In this work, we propose MUTE, an audio protection framework that uncouples the underlying audio-visual alignment through a multi-level strategy. Specifically, MUTE combines (1) Alignment-level Disruption, which directly perturbs cross-modal attention to disrupt structural alignment, and (2) Representation-level Degradation, which perturbs temporal audio embeddings to degrade their representations. To improve robustness, perturbations are constrained in the STFT domain to high-energy regions, making them resistant to post-processing, denoising, and adaptive attacks. An optional speaker-level objective further mitigates potential bypass via TTS-based resynthesis. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MUTE consistently degrades lip synchronization across both white-box and black-box talking-head models while preserving perceptual audio quality. The proposed method remains effective under real-world transformations and can be combined with image-based approaches to provide stronger multimodal protection. The source code and project page are available at https://github.com/jindl465/MUTE.

title: Horizon-Scalable Q-Learning
summary: Learning accurate off-policy state-action value functions (Q-functions) from offline datasets becomes harder as the task horizon grows. One-step temporal-difference (TD) learning bootstraps after every transition, so small per-step errors accumulate along the horizon, and early states can be badly misvalued even when the TD loss is small. Multi-step TD shortens this chain by following the dataset trajectory for several steps; however, since the behavior policy is often suboptimal, every followed action adds a bias, and no fixed number of steps suits a whole trajectory. In this paper, we propose Horizon-Scalable Q-Learning (HQL), a simple method that enables accurate long-horizon value learning by automatically balancing between one-step and multi-step returns. HQL extends a target through a dataset action only when the critic values it at least as highly as the best-of-N actions sampled from the BC policy, and otherwise falls back to a one-step target. We show that this rule is a principled off-policy correction that needs no action densities, which makes HQL compatible with expressive flow and diffusion policies. Experiments show that HQL avoids the failures of both one-step and multi-step TD on a combination-lock task across horizons, and outperforms prior horizon-reduction methods on long-horizon OGBench and OCBench tasks.

title: EmoHarness: Boosting Multimodal Emotion Understanding with Meta-Harness Evolving
comment: 18 pages, 11 figures, 6 tables. Project page: https://emo-harness.github.io. Code: https://github.com/Emo-Harness/EmoHarness
summary: Small multimodal models can misjudge emotion when words, voice, and visual cues conflict. We present EmoHarness, which runs such a model, the frozen student, inside a harness: the prompts, settings, and verification code around its calls. A human-written starting harness, the scaffold, numbers the student's visual observations, transcript, and prosody descriptions as citable evidence and has the student weigh candidate emotions against it. In Meta-Harness Evolving (MHE), a stronger LLM, the Builder, reads the student's errors and execution traces offline and edits the harness; static checks and validation gates decide which edits are kept, and the Builder never sees evaluation items. On 5,507 MME-Emotion items, EmoHarness raises task-macro Recognition by 7.6-13.4 points over a single video-only call for all four students and both Builders. Transcripts and prosody descriptions supply most of this boost (+5.38 to +10.71); the scaffold changes the audio-augmented call by -0.79 to +2.54, partly through extra multi-label predictions, and evolved edits add at most +0.95, although no evolved increment survives Holm correction. The harness's emotion context also transfers to IntentQA, with small gains for three of four students, none of which survives correction. EmoHarness thus boosts small multimodal students chiefly by supplying and organizing audio-derived evidence.

title: Differentiable Agent-Based Modeling for Multi-Echelon Supply Chains: Gradient-Based Optimization of Heterogeneous Policies at Scale
comment: 13 pages, 3 figures, 2026 Annual Modeling and Simulation Conference
summary: Global supply chains rely on the interactions of thousands of heterogeneous agents, posing significant challenges for optimization. While traditional optimization often assumes homogeneity to ensure tractability, Reinforcement Learning struggles with sample inefficiency when scaling to high-dimensional state spaces. We propose a Differentiable Agent-Based Model for multi-echelon inventory management. By implementing stochastic dynamics via differentiable tensor operations, we enable direct gradient propagation through the simulation. We validate the framework by recovering theoretical Newsvendor optima without supervision. Crucially, we demonstrate ``Mass Personalization'' by optimizing 10,000 distinct agent policies simultaneously in seconds, achieving a 53% cost reduction compared to scalar baselines. Furthermore, we utilize gradient sensitivity analysis to generate causal heatmaps, accurately recovering inherent lead-time delays from the computation graph. This approach bridges the gap between simulation and optimization, enabling the efficient training of self-correcting Digital Twins.

title: DPGS-SLAM: Diffusion-Prior and Provenance-Aware Monocular Gaussian Splatting SLAM for Dynamic Visual Sensing
summary: This paper presents DPGS-SLAM (Diffusion-Prior and Provenance-Aware Monocular Gaussian Splatting SLAM) for dense mapping in environments containing dynamic objects. Dynamic observations can contaminate camera tracking and scene reconstruction in visual SLAM (simultaneous localization and mapping). Although 3DGS (3D Gaussian splatting) enables efficient dense mapping, existing 3DGS-SLAM systems may exhibit instability when dynamic objects violate their underlying static-scene assumption. Excluding dynamic observations can reduce their influence on tracking and mapping, but may leave occluded static backgrounds missing or weakly constrained. Our proposed DPGS-SLAM is a monocular RGB SLAM framework that supports provisional representations of insufficiently observed static backgrounds through asynchronous diffusion-based background completion and provenance-aware Gaussian mapping. Dynamic regions are identified through optical-flow-based motion discovery and temporally consistent mask propagation by SAM2 (segment anything model 2). For selected keyframes, a fine-tuned diffusion inpainting model generates plausible background appearance in occluded regions, while Metric3D v2 predicts metric depth from the completed images to initialize provisional Gaussian primitives. Provenance labels distinguish generated primitives from observation-supported primitives, excluding generated content from camera-pose estimation and observed-map optimization. When previously occluded backgrounds become visible, eligible generated primitives are removed, and observation-supported primitives are independently initialized from real RGB observations and predicted depth. Experimental results demonstrated competitive camera tracking, with average ATE RMSE values of 1.2 cm on TUM RGB-D and 2.7 cm on BONN RGB-D. On StaDy4D, DPGS-SLAM improved average PSNR by 4.60 dB over WildGS-SLAM using only monocular RGB input.

title: GradReason: LLMs as Meta-Learners that Replace Training Epochs with Training-Data-Free Weight Updates
summary: Standard training recipes make a fixed number of passes over the training data, even when an epoch mostly adds mini-batch noise. We study whether a large language model (LLM) that reads the weight and gradient history of a run can replace some of these epochs with updates that compute no gradient and read no training image. In GradReason, an LLM agent is called every ten epochs. In a restricted sandbox, it analyses recent weight snapshots, epoch-mean gradients, and validation metrics, then submits a Python program that computes new weights and a plan marking each of the next ten epochs as data or virtual. A virtual epoch is kept only if it passes a forward-only check on 5,000 held-out validation images. In 120 runs on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 with three architectures, Claude Opus 5.5 used 32.8% fewer data epochs than the 80-epoch recipe at 0.31 percentage points lower test accuracy (95% CI -0.72 to +0.09; 0.94 points on ResNet-18), on the recipe's own frontier of data against accuracy. Unprompted, Opus averaged recent weight snapshots in every run. This choice produced the savings: a fixed rule with the same acceptance check but extrapolations from prior work saved 5.4% of the data epochs, and the same rule with averaging added saved 25.0%. The LLM's contribution is to find a working update within a single run; once found, a fixed rule implements it equally well. An Opus run cost 0.68 USD, but at this scale the agent's latency exceeded the GPU time it saved.

title: Leveraging High-Activity Post-Therapeutic I-131 Scans for Deep Learning Reconstruction of Extremely Sparse Planar Images in Differentiated Thyroid Cancer
summary: Background: Diagnostic I-131 whole-body planar imaging in differentiated thyroid cancer (DTC) is count-limited by low administered activity, and quality worsens under rapid acquisition. Models trained on such data struggle because their targets lack photon statistics. Purpose: To test whether high-quality post-therapeutic (PT) I-131 scans can serve as superior training references for enhancing sparse diagnostic planar images, using transfer learning and input-image addition. Methods: In this single-center prospective study, 111 patients were enrolled in PT training (n = 19), diagnostic follow-up (FU) training (n = 58), and FU paired test (n = 34) cohorts. Five Restormer-based models were trained: FU_DLx2 on FU labels; PT_DLx2 transfer-learned on PT data; PT_DLx1+ and PT_DLx2+ with input-image addition; PT_DLx6 as a PT-only reference. Test-time processing used two-step denormalization and Poisson re-scaling to preserve noise statistics. Quality was assessed by PSNR, SSIM, and a blinded dual-reader evaluation of all 34 test-cohort patients. Results: PT_DLx2 achieved the highest PSNR (34.4 +/- 3.6 dB) and SSIM (0.81 +/- 0.07). PT_DLx1+ and PT_DLx2+ were comparable (33.8 and 33.3 dB; SSIM 0.80). FU_DLx2 ranked below the unprocessed fast scan (30.3 vs. 32.0 dB; 0.76 vs. 0.79). Subjectively, PT_DLx2+ scored highest in image quality (4.54 +/- 0.60) and diagnostic confidence (4.54 +/- 0.60), surpassing the reference standard (4.19 +/- 0.83 and 4.31 +/- 0.81; P = 0.005 and P = 0.008). FU_DLx2 and PT_DLx6 scored lowest. Conclusion: Count-rich PT scans provide effective training priors for reconstructing extremely sparse images. Input-image addition and cross-domain transfer learning from PT data outperformed direct training on count-limited diagnostic data, supporting 2x scan acceleration with quality matching or exceeding the unaccelerated standard scan for selected PT-derived configurations.

title: PIA: Agentic Physics-Informed Runtime Anomaly Detection
summary: Runtime anomaly detectors for cyber-physical systems are either learned as black boxes from normal data, which miss stealthy manipulations that keep every signal inside its normal range, or derived by hand from physical models, which requires expert effort for every plant. We introduce physicsinformed agents (PIA), in which a large language model agent writes the detector itself as a set of physical residuals, such as pump characteristics, tank mass balances, and controller logic, and refines every candidate against normal operating data through an evaluation workbench before deployment. The result is a compact, human-readable detector that runs in milliseconds and names the component behind each alarm. On the BATADAL water distribution attack benchmark, PIA with Claude Opus 5.5 reaches an F1 of 0.878 on the test attacks against 0.504 for the strongest of six statistical and deep baselines, keeps detecting attacks concealed by replayed and offset sensor readings, and attributes every detected test attack to the attacked component. Ablations show that testing hypotheses against data is decisive: agents that write residuals from the plant description alone lose up to 0.28 F1, whereas agents that see only anonymized signals recover most of the physical structure.

title: SPARK: Simple Post-training for Adapting pRetrained Knowledge to Robot Control
summary: Large-scale representation learning has produced public foundation models that provide strong general-purpose visual features. However, their pretraining objectives are not designed for robot representation learning, so the resulting embeddings tend to emphasize global semantics rather than the temporally sensitive representations required for robot control. Training robot models from scratch is also undesirable due to the limited scale and high collection cost of robotics data, as well as the substantial computational burden of pre-training. In this paper, we propose SPARK (Simple Post-training for Adapting pRetrained Knowledge), a post-training method that adapts foundation models to robot control. SPARK is built on two principles: temporal abstraction, which encourages the encoder to derive compact features that preserve information essential for understanding temporal changes and action-relevant scene structure, and knowledge preservation, which aligns patch-level representations with those of the original foundation model to retain useful pretrained semantics. These objectives yield compact visual state representations that remain semantically meaningful while preserving useful prior knowledge. Experiments across multiple robotics benchmarks show that SPARK consistently improves success rates and generalization over vanilla foundation models, and further demonstrate that these gains transfer to real-world robot manipulation.

title: Slim Foundation Models for Latency-Critical Recommendation Serving
summary: Click-through rate (CTR) prediction is a core component of recommendation and advertising systems. Large language models (LLMs) offer rich semantic priors that improve prediction quality, particularly in cold-start and long-tail settings. Injecting a full-scale LLM into a CTR pipeline is, however, prohibitively expensive at inference time: existing LLM-enhanced CTR methods avoid this cost by caching LLM outputs offline rather than serving the LLM online. We propose a resource-efficient pipeline, SlimFM, that makes online LLM-based semantic modeling practical: (1) dependency-aware structured pruning compresses LLaMA3-8B by 44% to a 4.5B-parameter backbone; (2) LoRA-based field-aware fine-tuning trains the pruned model to produce discriminative field-level semantic embeddings from lightweight textual prompts; (3) a semantic-guided fusion module injects these embeddings into the feature interactions of a conventional CTR model. Across four datasets and six CTR backbones, SlimFM retains over 99% of uncompressed-model accuracy while reducing inference latency by up to 3.4x relative to existing LLM-enhanced baselines.

title: Real-Time Volumetric Light Transport Inference without a Path
summary: We present a real-time method for reconstructing fully integrated pixel radiance in rendered volumetric media under direct and ambient environmental illumination, using compact, low-cost scene features and statistics.
